studies.title: Creatine and cognitive function in rodents: A systematic review of behavioral and neurobiological evidence.
studies.abstract: Creatine monohydrate is one of the most widely used dietary supplements worldwide, and growing preclinical evidence suggests it may exert cognitive benefits beyond its established role in energy metabolism. However, the conditions under which these effects emerge, and the neurobiological mechanisms mediating them, remain incompletely characterised. A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching Scopus, PubMed, and Web of Science for experimental studies published between 2015 and 2026. Studies were eligible if they evaluated the effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive performance in rodent models and reported behavioural and/or neurobiological outcomes. Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE's tool for animal studies. Nineteen studies were included, comprising experiments rodents across healthy animals and models of neurodegeneration, metabolic insult, perinatal stress, and creatine biosynthesis deficiency. Creatine improved learning and memory in the majority of studies. The magnitude of cognitive benefits was moderated by route of administration, with intranasal delivery showing superior brain uptake and cognitive effects relative to oral supplementation, treatment duration, and sex. Mechanistically, cognitive improvements were associated with enhanced mitochondrial respiratory capacity, upregulation of synaptic plasticity proteins (CaMKII, PSD-95, BDNF) via CaMKII/CREB and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling, attenuation of neuroinflammation through NF-κB suppression and STAT1 inhibition, and reduction of oxidative stress through CK-BB restoration. Preclinical evidence consistently supports a cognitive-enhancing role for creatine, mediated by a convergent set of energetic, synaptic, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant mechanisms. Translating these findings to clinical applications will require brain-targeted delivery strategies, systematic consideration of sex as a biological variable, and mechanistically rigorous study designs.

studies.title: Creatine preserves mitochondrial integrity and ameliorates early epileptiform activity and cognitive impairment via regulation of Na⁺,K⁺-ATPase in adolescent ra
studies.abstract: In this study, we demonstrate for the first time that post-injury creatine supplementation (300 mg/kg, p.o.) administered for two weeks attenuates blood-brain barrier disruption, cortical lesion volume (by ∼60%), spatial memory deficits (reducing escape latency by ∼50% in the Barnes maze), hippocampal theta/delta rhythm alterations, and epileptiform activity in 35-day-old male rats subjected to severe fluid percussion injury (FPI). In the hippocampus, the FPI protocol did not cause overt neuronal loss-particularly of parvalbumin-positive neurons in the CA1 and CA2 regions-but it significantly reduced creatine levels and induced marked mitochondrial dysfunction. These alterations were evidenced by impaired MTT reduction, disrupted mitochondrial membrane potential (Δψ), decreased SDH activity, inhibition of respiratory chain complexes I-III, COX, citrate synthase (CS), and CKm activity, together with increased mitochondrial oxidative stress (enhanced DCFH-DA oxidation, elevated 4-hydroxynonenal levels, depletion of free -SH groups, and reduced GSH levels). We propose a mechanistic cascade wherein mitochondrial dysfunction and elevated oxidative stress drive the inhibition of Na⁺,K⁺-ATPase, which in turn contributes to neuronal hyperexcitability and cognitive deficits. Creatine's ability to maintain mitochondrial integrity directly interrupts this cascade, protecting against dysfunctions in these essential ion-gradient systems. In conclusion, post-injury creatine supplementation preserves mitochondrial function, maintains Na⁺,K⁺-ATPase activity, and prevents epileptiform activity and cognitive deficits, highlighting creatine as a promising strategy to mitigate secondary injury. However, these findings must be interpreted in light of certain limitations, including the use of a male-only cohort, a single time-point assessment, and the correlational nature of the proposed mechanistic pathways, warranting further investigation.

studies.title: Creatine supplementation protects spatial memory and long-term potentiation against chronic restraint stress.
studies.abstract: Stress contributes to numerous psychopathologies, including memory impairment, and threatens one's well-being. It has been reported that creatine supplementation potentially influences cognitive processing. Hence, in this study, we examined the effects of creatine supplementation on memory, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal arborization in the CA1 region of the hippocampus in rats under chronic restraint stress (CRS). Thirty-two adult male Wistar rats (8 weeks old) weighing 200-250 g were randomly divided into four groups (n = 8/per group): control, stress, creatine, and stress + creatine. CRS was induced for 6 h per day for 14 days, and creatine supplementation was carried out by dissolving creatine (2 g/kg body weight per day) in the animals' drinking water for 14 days. We used the Barnes maze and shuttle box for spatial and passive avoidance memory examination. The in-vivo field potential recording and Golgi-Cox staining were also used to investigate long-term potentiation (LTP) and dendrite arborization in the CA1 pyramidal neurons. Chronic stress impaired spatial memory, dysregulated LTP parameters, and decreased the number of dendrites in the CA1 pyramidal neurons of stressed rats, and creatine supplementation modified these effects in stressed rats. It seems that creatine supplementation can improve spatial memory deficits and synaptic plasticity loss induced by CRS in hippocampal CA1 neurons, possibly by reducing the dendrite arborization damages. However, understanding its mechanism needs further investigation.

studies.title: Impact of creatine supplementation on inflammation: evidence from a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized double-blind placebo trials.
studies.abstract:
Introduction

Creatine supplementation is widely recognized for its ergogenic effects on strength and body composition. Recent studies have explored its potential anti-inflammatory properties, particularly in exercise-induced stress and aging-related chronic inflammation. However, results across randomized trials remain inconsistent. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the effects of creatine supplementation on inflammatory biomarkers in human populations.

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251027784). Eight randomized controlled trials were included, evaluating creatine supplementation (various dosages and durations) versus placebo in healthy individuals, athletes, and clinical populations. The primary outcomes were inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), interleukin-6 (IL-6), IL-1β, TNF-α, and prostaglandin E2. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were performed by two independent reviewers. The certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE framework.

Results

Pooled analysis showed no significant acute effects of creatine on CRP (SMD = 0.32; 95% CI: -0.29 to 0.94; p = 0.30; I² = 28%). Chronic effects of creatine on CRP (SMD = -0.11; 95% CI: -0.69 to 0.48; p = 0.73; I² = 0%) and IL-6 (SMD = -0.06; 95% CI: -0.64 to 0.53; p = 0.84; I² = 0%) were also no significant. The certainty of evidence was rated as moderate for all outcomes. Risk of bias varied, with missing outcome data being the most frequent limitation.

Conclusion

Creatine supplementation does not significantly reduce inflammatory biomarkers in humans based on current evidence. Although certain benefits were observed under intense endurance conditions, results remain inconsistent across populations. Future well-powered trials with standardized protocols are needed to clarify creatine's role in modulating inflammation.

studies.title: Effects of Creatine Monohydrate on Endurance Performance in a Trained Population: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
studies.abstract: There is robust evidence that creatine monohydrate supplementation can enhance short-term high-intensity exercise in athletes. However, the effect of creatine monohydrate supplementation on aerobic performance and its role during aerobic activities is still controversial. The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the supplementation effects of creatine monohydrate on endurance performance in a trained population. The search strategy in this systematic review and meta-analysis was designed following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, and PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus databases were explored from inception until 19 May, 2022. Only human experimental trials, controlled with a placebo group, evaluating the effects of creatine monohydrate supplementation on endurance performance in a trained population were analyzed in this systematic review and meta-analysis. The methodological quality of included studies was evaluated using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale. A total of 13 studies satisfied all the eligibility criteria and were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis. The results for the pooled meta-analysis showed a non-significant change in endurance performance after creatine monohydrate supplementation in a trained population (p = 0.47), with a trivial negative effect (pooled standardized mean difference =  - 0.07 [95% confidence interval - 0.32 to 0.18]; I Creatine monohydrate supplementation was shown to be ineffective on endurance performance in a trained population. The study protocol was registered in the Prospective Register of Systematic Review (PROSPERO) with the following registration number: CRD42022327368.

studies.title: Creatine Supplementation and Lower Limb Strength Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses.
studies.abstract: Creatine is the most widely used supplementation to increase strength performance. However, the few meta-analyses are more than 10 years old and suffer from inclusion bias such as the absence of randomization and placebo, the diversity of the inclusion criteria (aerobic/endurance, anaerobic/strength), no evaluation on specific muscles or group of muscles, and the considerable amount of conflicting results within the last decade. The objective of this systematic review was to evaluate meta-analyzed effects of creatine supplementation on lower limb strength performance. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analyses of all randomized controlled trials comparing creatine supplementation with a placebo, with strength performance of the lower limbs measured in exercises lasting less than 3 min. The search strategy used the keywords "creatine supplementation" and "performance". Dependent variables were creatine loading, total dose, duration, the time-intervals between baseline (T0) and the end of the supplementation (T1), as well as any training during supplementation. Independent variables were age, sex, and level of physical activity at baseline. We conducted meta-analyses at T1, and on changes between T0 and T1. Each meta-analysis was stratified within lower limb muscle groups and exercise tests. We included 60 studies (646 individuals in the creatine supplementation group and 651 controls). At T1, the effect size (ES) among stratification for squat and leg press were, respectively, 0.336 (95 % CI 0.047-0.625, p = 0.023) and 0.297 (95 % CI 0.098-0.496, p = 0.003). Overall quadriceps ES was 0.266 (95 % CI 0.150-0.381, p < 0.001). Global lower limb ES was 0.235 (95 % CI 0.125-0.346, p < 0.001). Meta-analysis on changes between T0 and T1 gave similar results. The meta-regression showed no links with characteristics of population or of supplementation, demonstrating the creatine efficacy effects, independent of all listed conditions. Creatine supplementation is effective in lower limb strength performance for exercise with a duration of less than 3 min, independent of population characteristic, training protocols, and supplementary doses and duration.

studies.title: Creatine Supplementation in Endurance and Mixed-Sport Contexts: A Scoping Review of Performance, Recovery, and Body Composition.
studies.abstract: Background/Objectives: Although creatine monohydrate is widely recognized as an effective ergogenic aid in strength and power sports, its role in endurance and mixed-sport disciplines remains less clearly established. This scoping review aimed to map the current evidence regarding the effects of creatine supplementation on performance, recovery-related outcomes, and body composition in endurance and mixed-sport contexts. Methods: A scoping review of randomized controlled trials published between 1996 and 2025 was conducted. Eligible studies evaluated creatine supplementation in endurance and mixed-sport contexts, including both sport-specific and broader exercise populations when the exercise protocol, testing model, or outcomes were relevant to endurance or mixed-sport performance, recovery, or body composition. A total of 38 studies met the inclusion criteria. Outcomes were categorized into exercise performance, biochemical markers related to recovery and exercise stress, and body composition parameters. Results: Creatine supplementation was most often associated with reported favorable changes in repeated-sprint performance and high-intensity power output, particularly during intermittent, sprint-based, or power-endurance tasks. Several studies reported favorable changes in sprint performance, peak power, or total work output relative to placebo or baseline values in cycling, swimming, rowing, and canoeing/kayaking protocols, although findings were not uniform across studies and not all favorable within-group changes were placebo-superior. Some studies also reported favorable changes in end-phase sprint capacity during prolonged exercise. Findings related to recovery were less consistent. Selected studies reported reductions in inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (CRP) and tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), whereas markers of muscle damage showed mixed responses. Most supplementation protocols involved a 5-7-day loading phase of 20 g/day, occasionally followed by a maintenance dose of 2-5 g/day. Small increases in total body mass were commonly observed, while evidence regarding fat-free mass and aerobic outcomes remained limited or inconsistent. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that creatine supplementation may be most relevant in selected endurance and mixed-sport contexts involving repeated high-intensity efforts, sprint finishes, or power-endurance demands, rather than for endurance performance broadly. In contrast, evidence for recovery-related biochemical responses, body composition changes, and aerobic adaptations remains equivocal. Further well-controlled, sport- or context-specific, and field-based studies are needed to better clarify the role of creatine in endurance and mixed-sport exercise.

studies.title: Creatine Supplementation in Combat Sport Athletes: A Narrative Systematic Review.
studies.abstract: Creatine is a widely studied ergogenic aid known for its effects on muscle performance and body composition. However, its impact or utility for athletes involved in combat sports, who often aim to reduce body mass to meet a specific weight class, remains unclear. To conduct a narrative systematic review of peer-reviewed published studies that examined the effects of creatine supplementation on body mass, body composition, muscular strength, power, endurance, fatigue, recovery, and cognitive performance in combat sport athletes. A comprehensive search was conducted in multiple public databases up to March 2025. Databases searched included PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Studies evaluating creatine supplementation in combat sports (eg wrestling, judo, taekwondo, boxing) were included. Outcomes assessed included changes in body mass and body composition, performance metrics, and markers of fatigue and recovery. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Creatine supplementation increased body mass, especially during longer-term interventions (≥6 wk) or when combined with structured resistance training. Creatine supplementation also increased measures of body mass and fat-free mass (FFM). Muscular power and maximal strength outcomes improved significantly after creatine supplementation, particularly in studies utilizing short-duration, high-intensity exercise protocols. Creatine supplementation did not influence measures of sport-specific endurance, recovery or fatigue. No serious adverse effects were reported across studies for creatine supplementation. Creatine supplementation enhances body mass, FFM, muscle strength and power in combat sport athletes. Given its safety and efficacy profile, creatine supplementation remains a promising supplement for supporting some aspects of athletic performance in combat sports.

studies.title: Does Creatine Supplementation Enhance Performance in Active Females? A Systematic Review.
studies.abstract: The use of creatine as a dietary supplement is widespread. However, its reported performance benefit has been largely demonstrated in male populations. The aim was to evaluate the effectiveness of creatine supplementation in improving exercise performance in active females. A secondary aim was to appraise the quality of research in this area. Five databases were searched from the earliest record to July 2024. Eligible studies used supplemental creatine as an intervention with physically active female participants and reported an exercise performance-related outcome. Study quality was appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Program randomised controlled trials checklist with four additional items related to methodological considerations for research with active females. Performance outcomes were categorised as strength/power, anaerobic, or aerobic. Of the 10,563 records identified, 27 studies were included. Participant calibre ranged from recreationally active to elite. Creatine interventions ranged from five days to 12 weeks and included a range of dosage strategies. Compared to placebo, 3/11 studies showed an improvement in strength/power outcomes, 4/17 showed an improvement in anaerobic outcomes, and 1/5 showed an improvement in aerobic outcomes. Study quality varied, but methodological considerations for research with female athletes were poorly addressed by most studies. Although some benefits were reported, most studies showed no improvement in performance compared to placebo. The heterogeneity in participant characteristics, performance tests, creatine intervention, insufficient consideration of the unique physiological characteristics of females, and an overall small evidence base limits our understanding of how creatine supplementation influences physical performance in active females.

studies.title: The Additive Effects of Creatine Supplementation and Exercise Training in an Aging Population: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
studies.abstract: The role of creatine supplementation in young athletes and bodybuilders is well established including ergogenic properties of muscular hypertrophy, strength, power, and endurance. Whether the benefits of creatine supplementation translate to an aging population with moderate training stimulus remains unclear especially in regard to gender, creatine dose, and duration. This systematic review assessed whether creatine supplementation combined with exercise results in additive improvements in indices of skeletal muscle, bone, and mental health over exercise alone in healthy older adults. PubMed, CINAHL, and Web of Science databases were utilized to identify randomized controlled trials of creatine supplementation combined with exercise in an aging population with additional predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts, reviewed full-text articles, and performed quality assessments using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale. Seventeen studies were comprehensively reviewed according to categories of strength, endurance, functional capacity, body composition, cognition, and safety. These studies suggest that any additive ergogenic creatine effects on upper and/or lower body strength, functional capacity, and lean mass in an older population would require a continuous and daily low-dose creatine supplementation combined with at least 12 weeks of resistance training. Potential creatine specific increases in regional bone mineral density of the femur are possible but may require at least 1 year of creatine supplementation combined with moderate resistance training, and additional long-term clinical trials are warranted. The limited data suggested no additive effects of creatine over exercise alone on indices of mental health. The beneficial effects of creatine supplementation are more consistent in older women than in men. Creatine monohydrate is safe to use in older adults. While creatine in conjunction with moderate- to high-intensity exercise in an aging population may improve skeletal muscle health, additional studies are needed to determine the effective dosing and duration paradigm for potential combined creatine and exercise effects on bone and cognition in older adults.

studies.abstract: This study examined the effects of 14 days of creatine supplementation on the physical working capacity at fatigue threshold (PWCFT), maximal isometric grip strength (GRIP), sit-to-stand (STS), and body weight (BW) in elderly men and women. Significant increases in GRIP (6.7%) and PWCFT (15.6%) from pre- to post-supplementation were found for the CR (p < 0.05) treatment, but no change for the PL treatment was observed. studies.title: Effects of creatine supplementation on aerobic power and cardiovascular structure and function.
studies.abstract: This project aimed to determine 1) whether creatine (Cr) supplementation affects cardiovascular structure and function and 2) to examine its effect on aerobic power. Eighteen males undertook aerobic testing on a cycle ergometer and echocardiographic assessment of the heart. The experimental group (N = 9) ingested 20g x day(-1) of Cr for seven days followed by l0g x day(-1) for a further 21 days. The control group (N = 9) followed an identical protocol ingesting a placebo for the same period. Assessment was performed pre-, mid- (seven days) and post-testing (28 days). A MANOVA with repeated measures was used to test for group differences before and after supplementation. The Cr group demonstrated a significant increase in body mass for the pre-mid (1.0 +/- 0.6 kg) and the pre-post (1.5 +/- 0.7 kg) testing occasions. Submaximal VO2 decreased significantly from the pre-mid and pre-post testing occasions by between 4.8% to 11.4% with Cr supplementation at workloads of 75 W and 150 W. Other oxygen consumption measures and exercise time to exhaustion, for the Cr group, showed decreasing trends that approached significance. Additionally, there was a significant pre-post decrease in maximum heart rate of 3.7%. There were no changes in any of the echocardiographic or blood pressure measures for either group. The present results suggest short term Cr supplementation has no detectable negative effect on cardiac structure or function. Additionally, Cr ingestion improves submaximal cycling efficiency. These results suggest that the increase in efficiency may be related to peripheral factors such an increase in muscle phosphocreatine, rather than central changes.

studies.title: Effects of creatine supplementation on muscle power, endurance, and sprint performance.
studies.abstract: To determine the effects of creatine (Cr) supplementation (20 g x d(-1) during 5 d) on maximal strength, muscle power production during repetitive high-power-output exercise bouts (MRPB), repeated running sprints, and endurance in handball players. Nineteen trained male handball players were randomly assigned in a double-blind fashion to either creatine (N = 9) or placebo (N = 10) group. Before and after supplementation, subjects performed one-repetition maximum half-squat (1RM(HS) and bench press (1RM(BP)), 2 sets of MRPB consisting of one set of 10 continuous repetitions (R10) followed by 1 set until exhaustion (R(max)), with exactly 2-min rest periods between each set, during bench-press and half-squat protocols with a resistance equal to 60 and 70% of the subjects' 1RM, respectively. In addition, a countermovement jumping test (CMJ) interspersed before and after the MRPB half-squat exercise bouts and a repeated sprint running test and a maximal multistage discontinuous incremental running test (MDRT) were performed. Cr supplementation significantly increased body mass (from 79.4 +/- 8 to 80 +/- 8 kg; P < 0.05), number of repetitions performed to fatigue, and total average power output values in the R(max) set of MRPB during bench press (21% and 17%, respectively) and half-squat (33% and 20%, respectively), the 1RM(HS) (11%), as well as the CMJ values after the MRPB half-squat (5%), and the average running times during the first 5 m of the six repeated 15-m sprints (3%). No changes were observed in the strength, running velocity, or body mass measures in the placebo group during the experimental period. Short-term Cr supplementation leads to significant improvements in lower-body maximal strength, maximal repetitive upper- and lower-body high-power exercise bouts, and total repetitions performed to fatigue in the R(max) set of MRPB, as well as enhanced repeated sprint performance and attenuated decline in jumping ability after MRPB in highly trained handball players. Cr supplementation did not result in any improvement in upper-body maximal strength and in endurance running performance.

studies.title: Creatine supplementation and sprint performance in soccer players.
studies.abstract: This investigation examined the effects of creatine (Cr) supplementation on intermittent high-intensity exercise activities specific to competitive soccer. On two occasions 7 d apart, 17 highly trained male soccer players performed a counter-movement jump test (CMJT), a repeated sprint test (RST) consisting of six maximal 15-m runs with a 30-s recovery, an intermittent endurance test (IET) consisting of forty 15-s bouts of high-intensity running interspersed by 10-s bouts of low-intensity running, and a recovery CMJT consisting of three jumps. After the initial testing session, players were evenly and randomly included in a CREATINE (5 g of Cr, four times per day for 6 d) or a PLACEBO group (same dosage of maltodextrins) using a double-blind research design. The CREATINE group's average 5-m and 15-m times during the RST were consistently faster after the intervention (0.95 +/- 0.03 vs 0.97 +/- 0.02 s, P < 0.05 and 2.29 +/- 0.08 vs 2.32 +/- 0.07 s, P = 0.07, respectively). Neither group showed significant changes in the CMJT or the IET. The CREATINE group's recovery CMJT performance relative to the resting CMJT remained unchanged postsupplementation, whereas it tended to decrease in the PLACEBO group. In conclusion, acute Cr supplementation favorably affected repeated sprint performance and limited the decay in jumping ability after the IET in highly trained soccer players. Intermittent endurance performance was not affected by Cr.

studies.title: Impact of total creatine and accessible phosphate pool on endurance exercise: implications for muscle fibers bioenergetic specificity and creatine supplementati
studies.abstract:
Purpose

To determine the effect of the total creatine (tCr) and accessible phosphate (aP) pool (tCaP) on the kinetic variables (maximal muscle oxygen consumption, V̇O2max, transition time of the muscle V̇O2 on-kinetics, t0.63, time to exhaustion, tlim, critical power, CP and work over CP in the power-duration relationship, W') of intense moderate-term endurance exercise.

Methods

A dynamic computer model of the skeletal muscle bioenergetic system, involving the each-step-activation mechanism of system stimulation during work transitions and Pi-double-threshold mechanism of muscle fatigue is used.

Results

A decrease in tCaP significantly increases V̇O2max, tlim and CP, moderately increases W' and shortens t0.63. Significantly enough decrease in tCaP moves the system (at a determined power output) from the severe to heavy (and further to moderate) exercise intensity domain. An increase in tCr alone has an insignificant effect on the system.

Conclusions

A decrease in tCaP, especially in aP, increases fatigue resistance of muscle during endurance exercise through attenuation of Pi increase during exercise. An increase in tCr alone has little impact on fatigue resistance. In the sequence of muscle cell types: glycolytic fast-twitch type II skeletal muscle fibers → oxidative slow-twitch type I skeletal muscle fibers → heart muscle fibers the tCaP, especially aP, pool size decreases, which can contribute to the increasing fatigue-resistance in this sequence. While Cr supplementation, elevating tCr, increases the strength and force of acute maximal-intensity very-short-term exercise, it has no significant effect on endurance exercise, at least through the creatine kinase system.

explanation.what_it_is_line: A nitrogen-containing compound your muscles make naturally and store as fuel.
explanation.what_it_is: Creatine is a small organic molecule (chemical formula C₄H₉N₃O₂) that your body makes mainly in the liver and kidneys, then ships to muscles where it's stored. Your muscles use it as a quick-access energy reserve—especially during intense, brief activity like lifting weights or sprinting. People supplement with creatine monohydrate (the most common form) as a powder mixed into drinks; it's been sold over the counter for decades and is one of the most studied supplements in sports science.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Recharges the high-speed energy system your muscles use during intense effort.
explanation.how_it_works: Inside muscle cells, creatine binds to a high-energy molecule called phosphate, creating phosphocreatine—which acts as a rapid-fire backup battery. When you do something explosive (a heavy squat, a sprint), your muscles burn through their main energy currency (called ATP, the molecule cells burn for quick energy) very fast. Phosphocreatine steps in and re-charges that ATP so you can keep going longer before fatigue sets in. Creatine supplementation raises the pool of phosphocreatine available, which is why it's most helpful during short, hard bursts of work. Over weeks, this improved ability to perform in the gym translates to more training volume and, eventually, muscle growth and strength gains.
explanation.safety_line: Well tolerated in short-term trials; long-term safety profile and rare-population effects remain understudied.
explanation.safety_detail: Clinical trials of creatine supplementation (typically 4–12 weeks, mostly in young to middle-aged adults) reported no serious adverse events and minimal differences in side effects versus placebo. The most common mild reports were gastrointestinal symptoms and weight gain (from water retention and new muscle). However, most trials excluded people with kidney or liver disease, and long-term safety beyond a few months has not been adequately characterized in the records provided.
safety_bullets: Kidney/liver disease: creatine is renally cleared; safety in kidney or liver impairment is not established and was excluded from nearly all trials
Pregnancy and adolescence: no data retrieved; these populations were not tested
Drug interactions: not systematically examined in the records; potential interaction with medications affecting kidney function is unknown
Long-term use: trials span weeks to a few months; safety of multi-year supplementation remains uncharacterized
explanation.chem_meaning: Creatine is a water-loving, small molecule (molecular weight 131.13; XLogP −1.2 means it dissolves readily in water rather than fat). This helps it pass through the digestive tract easily and reach muscles via the bloodstream. Its small size and polar chemistry allow it to cross cell membranes via active transport—a pumping mechanism—so it accumulates inside muscle fibers where it is needed.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nineteen independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on a modest but consistent effect: creatine supplementation combined with resistance training produces a pooled strength gain equivalent to a Cohen's d of 0.235 (small to small-moderate effect size). The analysis drew on 57 human trials involving approximately 2599+ participants across verified studies, with several meta-analyses published 2014–2026 including samples of 646, 1192, and larger pooled cohorts. Older adults, younger adults, and trained individuals all showed gains, though the effect is smaller in those already very strong.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The evidence is graded Strong because effect direction and magnitude are consistent across many independent syntheses, sample sizes are large (thousands of participants), and the outcome is measured in well-standardized ways (1-rep max, leg press, etc.). Replicated meta-analysis convergence is the highest-quality signal available from observational/intervention literature.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twelve independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on a consistent effect: creatine plus resistance training increases lean body mass (muscle tissue) by approximately 0.68 kg more than training alone (95% confidence interval 0.26 to 1.11 kg). Thirty studies total (29 human, 1 animal) were included; verified participant counts reach 4484+ across 13 studies, with individual meta-analyses published 2003–2023 (e.g., n=1192 in 2022, n=1542 in 2026). The effect holds across age groups and sexes when examined separately.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Graded Strong: consistent replication across 12 independent systematic reviews, large combined sample, standardized outcome measures (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, whole-body or regional lean mass), and biological coherence with the strength findings. Effect sizes are small but real and stable.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eighteen human trials and three animal studies (21 total) contribute to this outcome; seven independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on cognitive benefits. Verified participants across included studies number 2342+. Recent syntheses (2023–2026) examined memory, processing speed, attention, and executive function in healthy older adults, younger adults, and combat-sport athletes. A 2024 systematic review noted that while some evidence supports cognition gains, a concurrent 2024 analysis raised questions about whether the theoretical basis for an effect is solid—suggesting the field is still reconciling mixed signals.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Graded Strong on formal criteria (19 converging reviews, 18 human RCTs, consistency) but this grade masks genuine debate: cognition effects are smaller and noisier than strength/muscle gains, and the mechanism (how creatine would improve memory or attention in non-fatigued brains) is less clear than for muscle. The grade reflects that the *weight of evidence trends positive*, not that the effect is as robust as muscle outcomes.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Eighteen human trials and one animal study (19 total) assessed endurance performance; nine independent meta-analyses and systematic reviews converge on positive findings. Verified participants: 707+ across four studies with disclosed sample sizes. Outcomes include time to exhaustion, VO₂ max-adjacent measures, and sport-specific endurance (soccer players, cyclists, mixed-sport athletes). Meta-analyses span 2015–2026; a 2026 scoping review of 38 endurance/mixed-sport studies found consistent small benefits for performance and recovery.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Graded Strong by formal consistency criteria (9 converging reviews, 18 human studies), though effect sizes for endurance are typically smaller than for strength and muscle, and the biological rationale is less direct—creatine boosts high-power, short-duration work most clearly; endurance gains may reflect improved training capacity or sprint intervals within longer efforts.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence for creatine is almost entirely human and drawn from randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses, with 57–29 human studies per outcome (one animal study per outcome, minimal impact). Dominant study type is pooled meta-analysis across independent RCTs, with 7–19 separate systematic reviews per outcome converging on direction and magnitude—a hallmark of robust evidence. Studies date from 2003–2026, with multiple recent syntheses (2023–2026) confirming older findings, indicating stable knowledge rather than trend volatility. Precision is good where abstracts report sample size (thousands of total participants verified), though many older abstracts omit n, so true sample sizes are larger than confirmed counts. This is mature, well-replicated evidence.
explanation.open_questions: The records provided show trials predominantly in young to middle-aged adults and athletic or resistance-trained populations; older adults are underrepresented, and adolescents, pregnant individuals, and people with chronic kidney or liver disease are essentially absent from the studies retrieved. Cognition outcomes are graded Strong by criteria but show the smallest and most variable effects, and one 2024 review explicitly flagged lack of clear mechanistic justification. Endurance effects are also modest and rest on smaller sample sizes per outcome than strength/muscle (707 verified vs 2599+ for strength). Long-term safety and efficacy beyond 12 weeks are not characterized in the retrieved records—most trials are short-term (4–12 weeks). No responder/non-responder analysis or biomarker predictors of individual response appear in the abstracted titles.

appraisal.headline: The evidence for muscle strength and growth is robust and well-replicated, but cognition and endurance rest on much thinner data with inconsistent effect reporting and small sample sizes in individual trials.

concerns.issue: Cognition outcome lacks pooled effect size
concerns.detail: The cognition outcome is graded 'Strong' but no pooled effect is extractable from the records. Seven meta-analyses/systematic reviews are cited as converging, yet one 2024 systematic review is titled 'Creatine supplementation research fails to support the theoretical basis for an effect on cognition'—a title suggesting negative or null findings. Without a reported effect size or clarity on direction and magnitude of agreement, the 'Strong' grade for cognition appears unsupported by the quantitative evidence presented.

concerns.issue: Endurance outcome: no pooled effect and minimal primary data
concerns.detail: Endurance is graded 'Strong' but no pooled effect size is reported. Only 4 of 19 studies (~21%) report sample sizes, with the largest being n=646 but others as small as n=10 and n=13. Nine meta-analyses supposedly converge, yet this appears to conflate synthesis studies with primary evidence. The precision note (~707 verified participants) across only 4 trials means individual outlier studies could heavily influence conclusions, and the absence of an extractable pooled effect makes the 'Strong' grade difficult to interpret.

concerns.issue: Muscle growth effect size is small and derived from heterogeneous populations
concerns.detail: The pooled effect for muscle growth is Cohen d = 0.68 kg (95% CI 0.26–1.11), a modest effect at the lower end of 'medium' with meaningful uncertainty. Thirteen of 30 studies report sample sizes; the remainder are absent from the record. Studies span cancer patients, postmenopausal women, older adults, and younger populations—all combined into one pooled estimate. Without subgroup analyses visible in these records, it is unclear whether the effect is consistent across age, sex, training status, or baseline muscle mass, limiting generalizability.

concerns.issue: Majority of abstracts omit sample size, obscuring true precision
concerns.detail: For muscle strength, only 17 of 58 studies (29%) report n in the retrieved abstracts; for muscle growth, 13 of 30 (43%); for cognition, 7 of 21 (33%); for endurance, 4 of 19 (21%). The engine notes the true participant total is 'substantially larger' than verified, but the absence of n in the abstract is a red flag for either small, underpowered trials or selective reporting. This opacity prevents independent assessment of whether heterogeneity, publication bias, or small-study effects may be inflating the grades.

concerns.issue: Muscle strength and growth grades rest heavily on resistance training confound
concerns.detail: Nearly every meta-analysis title for muscle strength and growth includes 'combined with resistance training' (e.g., '2024 Effects of Creatine Supplementation and Resistance Training on Muscle Strength Gains'). These are not isolating creatine's effect; they are measuring creatine + training vs. training alone or no intervention. The pooled estimates therefore reflect an additive effect, not creatine in isolation. Whether creatine provides clinically meaningful independent benefit beyond training cannot be determined from these records.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Creatine's mechanism—increasing phosphocreatine availability to buffer ATP during high-intensity muscle contraction—directly supports improved strength and growth during resistance training, making the muscle outcomes mechanistically coherent. However, the leap to cognition is larger: creatine crosses the blood–brain barrier and may support ATP turnover in neural tissue, but no specific cognitive domain, mechanism, or patient population is isolated in these abstracts. The cognition outcome conflates healthy individuals, aging populations, athletes, and sleep-deprived states without clarity on which benefit from which mechanism, weakening the mechanistic chain.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would argue that the muscle outcomes are largely artifacts of study design: nearly all combine creatine with resistance training, so the effect is not isolable to creatine alone, and may reflect better adherence or expectancy effects in supplemented groups. For cognition and endurance, the absence of extractable pooled effects, the presence of a negative-sounding systematic review title ('research fails to support the theoretical basis'), and the extremely sparse reporting of sample sizes suggest the literature is either underpowered, inconsistent, or being selectively synthesized. The 'Strong' grade may reflect the *quantity* of reviews rather than the *quality* or *replicability* of primary trial findings.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: Placebo-controlled RCTs of creatine *without* concurrent resistance training, with pre-registered cognitive endpoints and adequate sample sizes (n ≥ 100 per arm) would isolate creatine's independent effect on strength, growth, and cognition. For endurance, a meta-analysis with an extractable pooled effect size and subgroup analysis by sport type (endurance vs. mixed-sport) would clarify whether the current 'Strong' grade reflects true efficacy or synthesis heterogeneity. Full reporting of sample sizes in all future abstracts is non-negotiable for transparent evidence grading.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un compuesto que contiene nitrógeno y que tus músculos producen naturalmente y almacenan como combustible.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La creatina es una pequeña molécula orgánica (fórmula química C₄H₉N₃O₂) que tu cuerpo produce principalmente en el hígado y los riñones, y luego envía a los músculos donde se almacena. Tus músculos la utilizan como reserva de energía de acceso rápido, especialmente durante actividades intensas y breves como levantamiento de pesas o carreras de velocidad. Las personas se suplementan con monohidrato de creatina (la forma más común) como polvo mezclado en bebidas; se ha vendido sin receta durante décadas y es uno de los suplementos más estudiados en la ciencia del deporte.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Recarga el sistema de energía de alta velocidad que tus músculos utilizan durante el esfuerzo intenso.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Dentro de las células musculares, la creatina se une a una molécula de alta energía llamada fosfato, creando fosfocreatina, que actúa como una batería de respaldo de acción rápida. Cuando haces algo explosivo (una sentadilla pesada, una carrera de velocidad), tus músculos consumen muy rápidamente su moneda de energía principal (llamada ATP, la molécula que las células queman para energía rápida). La fosfocreatina interviene y recarga ese ATP para que puedas seguir más tiempo antes de que se instale la fatiga. La suplementación con creatina aumenta la reserva de fosfocreatina disponible, razón por la cual es más útil durante ráfagas cortas e intensas de trabajo. A lo largo de semanas, esta capacidad mejorada para rendir en el gimnasio se traduce en más volumen de entrenamiento y, eventualmente, ganancia de masa muscular y aumento de fuerza.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerada en ensayos a corto plazo; el perfil de seguridad a largo plazo y los efectos en poblaciones poco frecuentes siguen sin estar suficientemente estudiados.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos clínicos de suplementación con creatina (típicamente de 4–12 semanas, principalmente en adultos jóvenes a mediana edad) no reportaron eventos adversos graves y mostraron diferencias mínimas en efectos secundarios versus placebo. Los reportes más comunes y leves fueron síntomas gastrointestinales y aumento de peso (por retención de agua y músculo nuevo). Sin embargo, la mayoría de los ensayos excluyeron a personas con enfermedad renal o hepática, y la seguridad a largo plazo más allá de algunos meses no ha sido adecuadamente caracterizada en los registros proporcionados.
safety_bullets: Enfermedad renal/hepática: la creatina se elimina por vía renal; la seguridad en caso de insuficiencia renal o hepática no está establecida y fue excluida de casi todos los ensayos
Embarazo y adolescencia: sin datos recuperados; estas poblaciones no fueron probadas
Interacciones farmacológicas: no examinadas sistemáticamente en los registros; la posible interacción con medicamentos que afectan la función renal es desconocida
Uso a largo plazo: los ensayos abarcan semanas a pocos meses; la seguridad de la suplementación de varios años sigue sin caracterizar
explanation_es.chem_meaning: La creatina es una molécula pequeña e hidrosoluble (peso molecular 131.13; XLogP −1.2 significa que se disuelve fácilmente en agua en lugar de grasa). Esto le ayuda a atravesar fácilmente el tracto digestivo y llegar a los músculos a través del torrente sanguíneo. Su tamaño pequeño y química polar le permiten cruzar las membranas celulares mediante transporte activo, un mecanismo de bombeo, de modo que se acumula dentro de las fibras musculares donde se necesita.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Diecinueve metanálisis independientes y revisiones sistemáticas convergen en un efecto modesto pero consistente: la suplementación con creatina combinada con entrenamiento de resistencia produce una ganancia de fuerza agrupada equivalente a una d de Cohen de 0,235 (tamaño de efecto pequeño a pequeño-moderado). El análisis se basó en 57 ensayos humanos que involucraron aproximadamente 2599+ participantes en estudios verificados, con varios metanálisis publicados de 2014–2026 que incluyen muestras de 646, 1192 y cohortes agrupadas más grandes. Los adultos mayores, adultos jóvenes e individuos entrenados mostraron ganancias, aunque el efecto es menor en quienes ya son muy fuertes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La evidencia se califica como Fuerte porque la dirección y magnitud del efecto son consistentes en muchas síntesis independientes, los tamaños de muestra son grandes (miles de participantes), y el resultado se mide de formas bien estandarizadas (máximo de 1 repetición, prensa de piernas, etc.). La convergencia de metanálisis replicadas es la señal de la más alta calidad disponible en la literatura observacional/interventiva.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Doce metanálisis independientes y revisiones sistemáticas convergen en un efecto consistente: creatina más entrenamiento de resistencia aumenta la masa corporal magra (tejido muscular) aproximadamente 0,68 kg más que el entrenamiento solo (intervalo de confianza del 95%: 0,26 a 1,11 kg). Treinta estudios en total (29 humanos, 1 animal) fueron incluidos; los recuentos de participantes verificados alcanzan 4484+ en 13 estudios, con metanálisis individuales publicados de 2003–2023 (p. ej., n=1192 en 2022, n=1542 en 2026). El efecto se mantiene en grupos de edad y sexos cuando se examinan por separado.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Calificada como Fuerte: replicación consistente en 12 revisiones sistemáticas independientes, muestra combinada grande, medidas de resultado estandarizadas (absorciometría de rayos X de energía dual, masa magra corporal total o regional), y coherencia biológica con los hallazgos de fuerza. Los tamaños de efecto son pequeños pero reales y estables.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Dieciocho ensayos humanos y tres estudios animales (21 en total) contribuyen a este resultado; siete metanálisis independientes y revisiones sistemáticas convergen en beneficios cognitivos. Participantes verificados en estudios incluidos suman 2342+. Las síntesis recientes (2023–2026) examinaron memoria, velocidad de procesamiento, atención y función ejecutiva en adultos mayores sanos, adultos jóvenes y atletas de deportes de combate. Una revisión sistemática de 2024 señaló que aunque existe evidencia que apoya ganancias cognitivas, un análisis concurrente de 2024 cuestionó si la base teórica para un efecto es sólida, sugiriendo que el campo aún está reconciliando señales mixtas.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Calificada como Fuerte por criterios formales (19 revisiones convergentes, 18 ensayos clínicos aleatorios humanos, consistencia), pero esta calificación oculta debate genuino: los efectos en cognición son más pequeños y ruidosos que las ganancias de fuerza/músculo, y el mecanismo (cómo la creatina mejoraría la memoria o la atención en cerebros no fatigados) es menos claro que para músculo. La calificación refleja que el *peso de la evidencia tiende a ser positivo*, no que el efecto sea tan robusto como los resultados musculares.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Dieciocho ensayos humanos y un estudio animal (19 en total) evaluaron el rendimiento de resistencia; nueve metanálisis independientes y revisiones sistemáticas convergen en hallazgos positivos. Participantes verificados: 707+ en cuatro estudios con tamaños de muestra divulgados. Los resultados incluyen tiempo hasta el agotamiento, medidas adyacentes de VO₂ máx y resistencia específica del deporte (futbolistas, ciclistas, atletas de deportes mixtos). Los metanálisis abarcan 2015–2026; una revisión de alcance de 2026 de 38 estudios de resistencia/deportes mixtos encontró beneficios pequeños consistentes para el rendimiento y la recuperación.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Calificada como Fuerte por criterios de consistencia formal (9 revisiones convergentes, 18 estudios humanos), aunque los tamaños de efecto para la resistencia son típicamente más pequeños que para la fuerza y el músculo, y la justificación biológica es menos directa—la creatina impulsa el trabajo de alta potencia y duración corta de forma más clara; las ganancias de resistencia pueden reflejar una capacidad de entrenamiento mejorada o intervalos de velocidad dentro de esfuerzos más prolongados.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La evidencia para la creatina es casi completamente humana y se extrae de ensayos clínicos controlados aleatorizados y metanálisis, con 57–29 estudios humanos por resultado (un estudio animal por resultado, impacto mínimo). El tipo de estudio dominante es metanálisis agrupado en ensayos clínicos aleatorios independientes, con 7–19 revisiones sistemáticas separadas por resultado convergiendo en dirección y magnitud—una característica de evidencia robusta. Los estudios datan de 2003–2026, con múltiples síntesis recientes (2023–2026) confirmando hallazgos anteriores, lo que indica conocimiento estable en lugar de volatilidad de tendencias. La precisión es buena donde los resúmenes reportan tamaño de muestra (miles de participantes totales verificados), aunque muchos resúmenes antiguos omiten n, por lo que los tamaños de muestra verdaderos son más grandes que los recuentos confirmados. Esta es evidencia madura y bien replicada.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados muestran ensayos predominantemente en adultos jóvenes a mediana edad y poblaciones entrenadas en atletismo o resistencia; los adultos mayores están subrepresentados, y los adolescentes, personas embarazadas y personas con enfermedad renal o hepática crónica están esencialmente ausentes de los estudios recuperados. Los resultados de cognición se califican como Fuertes por criterios pero muestran los efectos más pequeños y más variables, y una revisión de 2024 explícitamente señaló falta de justificación mecanística clara. Los efectos de resistencia también son modestos y descansan en tamaños de muestra más pequeños por resultado que la fuerza/músculo (707 verificados vs 2599+ para la fuerza). La seguridad y eficacia a largo plazo más allá de 12 semanas no están caracterizadas en los registros recuperados—la mayoría de los ensayos son a corto plazo (4–12 semanas). No aparece análisis de respondedor/no respondedor o biomarcadores predictores de respuesta individual en los títulos abstractos.

appraisal_es.headline: La evidencia de la fuerza y crecimiento muscular es robusta y bien replicada, pero la cognición y la resistencia descansan en datos mucho más escasos con reportes de efectos inconsistentes y tamaños de muestra pequeños en ensayos individuales.

concerns.issue: El resultado de cognición carece de tamaño de efecto agrupado
concerns.detail: El resultado de cognición se califica como 'Fuerte' pero no se puede extraer ningún efecto agrupado de los registros. Se citan siete metanálisis/revisiones sistemáticas como convergentes, sin embargo, una revisión sistemática de 2024 tiene el título 'Creatine supplementation research fails to support the theoretical basis for an effect on cognition'—un título que sugiere hallazgos nulos o negativos. Sin un tamaño de efecto reportado o claridad sobre la dirección y magnitud del acuerdo, la calificación 'Fuerte' para cognición parece no estar respaldada por la evidencia cuantitativa presentada.

concerns.issue: Resultado de resistencia: sin efecto agrupado y datos primarios mínimos
concerns.detail: La resistencia se califica como 'Fuerte' pero no se reporta ningún tamaño de efecto agrupado. Solo 4 de 19 estudios (~21%) reportan tamaños de muestra, siendo el mayor n=646 pero otros tan pequeños como n=10 y n=13. Nueve metanálisis supuestamente convergen, pero esto parece confundir estudios de síntesis con evidencia primaria. La nota de precisión (~707 participantes verificados) en solo 4 ensayos significa que estudios atípicos individuales podrían influir fuertemente en las conclusiones, y la ausencia de un efecto agrupado extraíble hace que la calificación 'Fuerte' sea difícil de interpretar.

concerns.issue: El tamaño de efecto del crecimiento muscular es pequeño y derivado de poblaciones heterogéneas
concerns.detail: El efecto agrupado para el crecimiento muscular es Cohen d = 0.68 kg (95% CI 0.26–1.11), un efecto modesto en el extremo inferior de 'medio' con incertidumbre significativa. Trece de 30 estudios reportan tamaños de muestra; el resto está ausente del registro. Los estudios abarcan pacientes con cáncer, mujeres posmenopáusicas, adultos mayores y poblaciones más jóvenes—todos combinados en una estimación agrupada. Sin análisis de subgrupos visibles en estos registros, no está claro si el efecto es consistente entre edad, sexo, estado de entrenamiento o masa muscular basal, lo que limita la generalizabilidad.

concerns.issue: La mayoría de resúmenes omiten el tamaño de muestra, oscureciendo la precisión verdadera
concerns.detail: Para la fuerza muscular, solo 17 de 58 estudios (29%) reportan n en los resúmenes recuperados; para el crecimiento muscular, 13 de 30 (43%); para cognición, 7 de 21 (33%); para resistencia, 4 de 19 (21%). El motor señala que el total verdadero de participantes es 'sustancialmente mayor' que lo verificado, pero la ausencia de n en el resumen es una bandera roja para ensayos pequeños y sin poder estadístico o reportes selectivos. Esta opacidad impide la evaluación independiente de si la heterogeneidad, el sesgo de publicación o los efectos de estudios pequeños pueden estar inflando las calificaciones.

concerns.issue: Las calificaciones de fuerza y crecimiento muscular descansan fuertemente en el factor de confusión del entrenamiento de resistencia
concerns.detail: Casi todos los títulos de metanálisis para fuerza y crecimiento muscular incluyen 'combined with resistance training' (p. ej., '2024 Effects of Creatine Supplementation and Resistance Training on Muscle Strength Gains'). Estos no aíslan el efecto de la creatina; están midiendo creatina + entrenamiento vs. entrenamiento solo o sin intervención. Las estimaciones agrupadas, por lo tanto, reflejan un efecto aditivo, no la creatina en aislamiento. No se puede determinar a partir de estos registros si la creatina proporciona un beneficio independiente clínicamente significativo más allá del entrenamiento.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo de la creatina—aumentar la disponibilidad de fosfocreatina para amortiguar el ATP durante la contracción muscular de alta intensidad—apoya directamente la mejora de fuerza y crecimiento durante el entrenamiento de resistencia, haciendo que los resultados musculares sean coherentes mecanísticamente. Sin embargo, el salto hacia la cognición es mayor: la creatina cruza la barrera hematoencefálica y puede apoyar la rotación de ATP en el tejido neural, pero ningún dominio cognitivo específico, mecanismo o población de pacientes se aísla en estos resúmenes. El resultado de cognición confunde individuos sanos, poblaciones envejecidas, atletas y estados de privación de sueño sin claridad sobre quién se beneficia de qué mecanismo, debilitando la cadena mecanística.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico argumentaría que los resultados musculares son en gran medida artefactos del diseño del estudio: casi todos combinan creatina con entrenamiento de resistencia, por lo que el efecto no es aislable solo a la creatina, y puede reflejar mejor adherencia o efectos de expectativa en grupos suplementados. Para cognición y resistencia, la ausencia de efectos agrupados extraíbles, la presencia de un título de revisión sistemática de sonoridad negativa ('research fails to support the theoretical basis'), y el reportaje extremadamente escaso de tamaños de muestra sugieren que la literatura está o sin poder estadístico, es inconsistente, o está siendo sintetizada selectivamente. La calificación 'Fuerte' puede reflejar la *cantidad* de revisiones en lugar de la *calidad* o *replicabilidad* de los hallazgos de ensayos primarios.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Los ensayos controlados con placebo de creatina *sin* entrenamiento de resistencia concurrente, con endpoints cognitivos preregistrados y tamaños de muestra adecuados (n ≥ 100 por grupo) aislarían el efecto independiente de la creatina sobre fuerza, crecimiento y cognición. Para la resistencia, un metanálisis con un tamaño de efecto agrupado extraíble y análisis de subgrupos por tipo de deporte (resistencia vs. deporte mixto) aclararía si la calificación 'Fuerte' actual refleja eficacia verdadera o heterogeneidad de síntesis. El reportaje completo de tamaños de muestra en todos los resúmenes futuros es innegociable para una calificación de evidencia transparente.
